events.text: Rumi on Grief and Separation: When the Beloved Is Gone
events.sub: Eight Persian Sufi poems with English translation
events.fa: مولانا و غم هجران

events.text: Rumi knew loss. Shams of Tabriz, the friend who changed his life, disappeared and never came back.
Many of his most moving poems were written in that absence.
Here are eight passages about grief, separation, and the tears that make gardens grow.

events.fa: سینه خواهم شرحه‌شرحه از فراق
events.en: I want a heart torn piece by piece by separation,

events.fa: تا بگویم شرح درد اشتیاق
events.en: so that I can tell the pain of longing.

events.text: This is the reed flute speaking, in the opening of the Masnavi.
It does not want to explain longing to just anyone.
Only someone who has been torn by separation can understand it.
Grief makes us able to hear other people's grief. That is one of its strange gifts.

fa: سینه خواهم شرحه‌شرحه از فراق
تا بگویم شرح درد اشتیاق

events.fa: دست من گیر ای پسر خوش نیستم
events.en: Take my hand, young friend. I am not well.

events.fa: ای قد تو چون شجر خوش نیستم
events.en: O you, tall as a tree, I am not well.

events.fa: تا تو رفتی قوت و صبرم برفت
events.en: Since you left, my strength and my patience left;

events.fa: تا تو رفتی من دگر خوش نیستم
events.en: since you left, I have not been well.

events.text: These are some of the simplest words Rumi ever wrote.
No grand images. Only: take my hand, I am not well.
Grief often speaks like this, plainly, again and again.
There is no shame in saying it. Sometimes saying it is the first step toward being held.

fa: دست من گیر ای پسر خوش نیستم
ای قد تو چون شجر خوش نیستم
تا تو رفتی قوت و صبرم برفت
تا تو رفتی من دگر خوش نیستم

events.fa: رو سر بنه به بالین تنها مرا رها کن
events.en: Go, lay your head on the pillow, and leave me alone;

events.fa: ترک من خراب شبگرد مبتلا کن
events.en: leave me, ruined, wandering the night, afflicted.

events.fa: ماییم و موج سودا شب تا به روز تنها
events.en: Here I am with the waves of longing, alone from night till day.

events.fa: خواهی بیا ببخشا خواهی برو جفا کن
events.en: Come and forgive if you wish, or go and be cruel.

events.text: Many believe this ghazal was written in Rumi's last days.
He tells a loved one to go and sleep, and leave him with his sleeplessness.
Waves of longing all night. And no demand of the beloved: come, or go.
Grief can feel like this: too tired even to ask for anything.

fa: رو سر بنه به بالین تنها مرا رها کن
ترک من خراب شبگرد مبتلا کن
ماییم و موج سودا شب تا به روز تنها
خواهی بیا ببخشا خواهی برو جفا کن

events.fa: بر شاه خوبرویان واجب وفا نباشد
events.en: The king of the beautiful owes no faithfulness;

events.fa: ای زردروی عاشق تو صبر کن وفا کن
events.en: O pale-faced lover, you be patient, you be faithful.

events.fa: دردیست غیر مردن آن را دوا نباشد
events.en: There is a pain that has no cure but dying;

events.fa: پس من چگونه گویم کاین درد را دوا کن
events.en: so how can I say: cure this pain?

events.text: From the same ghazal, Rumi admits something hard.
Some pain cannot be fixed, and he will not pretend it can.
What is asked of the lover is not to be cured, but to stay faithful.
There is a dignity in that. Carrying a grief faithfully is also a form of love.

fa: بر شاه خوبرویان واجب وفا نباشد
ای زردروی عاشق تو صبر کن وفا کن
دردیست غیر مردن آن را دوا نباشد
پس من چگونه گویم کاین درد را دوا کن

events.fa: که از آن دم که تو سفر کردی
events.en: For since the moment you went away,

events.fa: از حلاوت جدا شدیم چو موم
events.en: we have been parted from sweetness, like wax from honey.

events.fa: همه شب همچو شمع می‌سوزیم
events.en: All night we burn like a candle,

events.fa: ز آتشش جفت وز انگبین محروم
events.en: joined to its fire and cut off from its honey.

events.text: Candles were made of beeswax, the wax that once held honey.
Rumi says: since you left, I am that wax. The honey is gone. Only the burning is left.
It is one of the most precise pictures of grief in Persian poetry.
Yet a candle that burns also gives light. Even this pain is not useless.

fa: که از آن دم که تو سفر کردی
از حلاوت جدا شدیم چو موم
همه شب همچو شمع می‌سوزیم
ز آتشش جفت وز انگبین محروم

events.fa: ز فراق جان من گر ز دو دیده در فشاند
events.en: If, from separation, my soul pours pearls from both eyes,

events.fa: تو گمان مبر که از وی دل پرگهر ندارم
events.en: do not imagine that my heart is no longer full of jewels.

events.text: In Persian poetry tears are often called pearls.
Rumi is weeping. But he says: do not think the weeping has emptied me.
The heart that weeps is still full.
Grief does not mean we have lost the treasure. It is often the sign of how much we still hold.

fa: ز فراق جان من گر ز دو دیده در فشاند
تو گمان مبر که از وی دل پرگهر ندارم

events.fa: توی شاها و دیرینه مقام تست این سینه
events.en: You are the king, and this chest has long been your home;

events.fa: نمی‌گویی کجا بودی که جان بی‌تو نزار آمد
events.en: will you not say where you were? Without you, the soul has grown thin.

events.text: Here the lover speaks to someone who has finally come back.
This heart was always your home, he says. Where were you?
There is reproach in it, and relief, and tenderness.
Grief and joy often meet at the door like this, when the absent one returns.

fa: توی شاها و دیرینه مقام تست این سینه
نمی‌گویی کجا بودی که جان بی‌تو نزار آمد

events.fa: گلستان و گل و ریحان نروید جز ز دست تو
events.en: Rose gardens, roses and sweet herbs grow only from your hand;

events.fa: دو چشمه داری ای چهره چرا پرنم نمی‌گردی
events.en: you have two springs, O face: why do you not fill with tears?

events.text: Rumi ends this ghazal with a surprising question.
Your two eyes are springs of water, he says. Why are they dry?
For him, tears are not weakness. They water the garden.
Let them come. What grows after grief can be more beautiful than what was there before.

fa: گلستان و گل و ریحان نروید جز ز دست تو
دو چشمه داری ای چهره چرا پرنم نمی‌گردی

events.text: Thank you for staying with these verses.
Every week we share real passages of Rumi, translated honestly from the Persian.
If they spoke to you, subscribe to The Guest House.
